paragraphs: This paper develops a common mathematical setting for studying message passing graph neural networks on sparse and dense graphs of arbitrary size. Earlier approaches faced a split: theories allowing unbounded graph sizes were appropriate for dense graphs, while theories addressing sparse graphs restricted how large the graphs could become. That separation limited what a single analysis could cover.

The authors construct a compact metric space that includes both kinds of graphs across all sizes. The metric provides a way to compare graph inputs, while equicontinuity ensures that the studied networks respond in a uniformly controlled way to changes measured by that metric. Their construction builds on and extends graphop analysis, an approach to graph limits.

The resulting framework supports stronger universal approximation theorems and generalization bounds than the previous approaches described in the abstract. Its contribution is theoretical: it broadens the graph settings in which approximation and generalization can be analyzed together, bringing sparse graphs of unrestricted size into the same framework as dense ones.
icml-2026-a-graphop-analysis-of-graph-ne.tldr: A graphop-based framework strengthens approximation and generalization theory for message passing networks on sparse and dense graphs of arbitrary size.

paragraphs: Prediction intervals need not extend equally far above and below a model's prediction. Noise can be skewed, and a biased model can produce uneven residuals even when the underlying noise is more balanced. This paper develops an adaptive conformal prediction procedure that accommodates these asymmetries while retaining a connection to symmetric intervals.

The central mechanism is a penalty that encourages symmetry. Changing its strength moves the learned prediction bands smoothly between symmetric and asymmetric forms. The learning problem uses reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and kernel sum-of-squares methods. Representer theorems make the formulation computationally tractable, and dual formulations support scaling it to larger datasets.

A data-driven method chooses the penalty strength by identifying symmetry in the noise. This makes the amount of permitted asymmetry something learned from data rather than fixed beforehand. The authors show that allowing some asymmetry can improve adaptation with small samples, outliers, or biased predictive models, and their experiments illustrate the method's effectiveness for learning adaptive prediction bands.
icml-2026-asymmetric-conformal-predictio.tldr: A data-selected symmetry penalty lets conformal prediction bands adapt smoothly to both balanced and skewed errors.

paragraphs: Two neural representations can look different while supporting the same task. This paper connects comparisons of internal representations with comparisons of what those representations let models do. Its organizing idea is usable information: similarity depends on the information that a specified family of predictors can extract, making the observer's capacity part of the comparison.

For functional similarity, the authors formally connect model stitching performance to conditional mutual information. They show that stitching is asymmetric, so testing a mapping in one direction does not provide a robust comparison by itself. For representational similarity, they interpret reconstruction metrics and tools such as CKA and RSA as estimators of usable information under particular constraints.

The framework establishes that representational similarity is sufficient, but not necessary, for functional similarity. It also organizes tasks by granularity: similarity on a complex task guarantees similarity on a coarser derivative of that task. Input reconstruction sits at the most detailed end of this hierarchy, explaining how closely matched representations can imply shared functionality without requiring every functionally similar pair to share equally similar representations.
icml-2026-bridging-functional-and-repres.tldr: Usable information connects representation similarity to shared functionality while showing why comparisons depend on predictor capacity and task granularity.

paragraphs: Mechanistic interpretability identifies small subnetworks, or circuits, associated with particular behaviors. However, a discovered circuit can depend heavily on the examples used to define the behavior. This paper addresses that instability by certifying whether decisions to include individual components survive bounded changes to the concept dataset.

Certified Circuits wraps an existing discovery algorithm with randomized data subsampling. Depending on the underlying algorithm, the components are neurons or edges in the model graph. The framework certifies invariance of component inclusion decisions under bounded edit-distance perturbations to the dataset. When a component's inclusion is unstable, the method abstains from including it rather than treating the discovery as dependable.

The authors evaluate the framework on ResNet, ViT, and GPT-2 across vision and language tasks, including distribution shifts. They report up to 56% higher accuracy and up to 80% fewer components. These empirical improvements accompany a specific formal guarantee about dataset perturbations, giving circuit explanations a measurable notion of stability alongside their observed accuracy and compactness.
icml-2026-certified-circuits-stability-g.tldr: Randomized subsampling certifies circuit-component stability under bounded dataset edits and yields smaller, more accurate circuits in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: This paper studies a bandit learner that must choose both an action and the data source used to observe rewards. Sources have different, initially unknown noise variances. Consequently, learning which action pays best is coupled to learning which source supplies the clearest evidence, creating an additional exploration problem.

The proposed SOAR algorithm manages both choices through confidence bounds. Upper bounds on arm rewards encourage exploration of potentially valuable actions, while lower bounds on source variances encourage investigation of potentially precise sources. The resulting strategy learns about reward quality and observation quality together instead of assuming the best source is already known.

The theoretical regret bound depends on the smallest source variance and the gaps between optimal and suboptimal rewards, up to polylogarithmic factors. A separate preprocessing cost grows at most logarithmically with the time horizon. In this qualified sense, SOAR matches the instance-dependent regret available from using the best source in advance. Synthetic experiments and MovieLens 32M evaluations also show significantly lower regret than the tested baseline bandit algorithms.
icml-2026-data-source-adaptive-online-le.tldr: SOAR jointly learns good actions and low-noise data sources, approaching best-source bandit regret without knowing that source beforehand.

paragraphs: Adversarial suffixes can remain fluent enough to evade detectors based on how surprising their wording looks. This paper instead follows changes in the model's next-token uncertainty as a prompt unfolds. It treats the beginning of an adversarial suffix as a change point in that sequential uncertainty signal.

The detector, CPD Online, estimates a robust baseline from the system prompt, standardizes entropies for user tokens, and accumulates departures using a one-sided CUSUM statistic. It requires no training and can operate online across models. Its output can identify both a suspicious prompt and the position where the suspicious suffix begins.

Across six chat models, CPD improves F1 over the strongest windowed-perplexity baseline on a benchmark with 1,012 attacks and equally many perplexity-controlled benign prompts. It places 79.6% of triggers inside adversarial suffixes, compared with 17–46% for windowed perplexity. Used as a gate for LLaMA Guard in a benign-dominated deployment, it reduces guard calls by 17–22% while preserving guard-level detection quality.
icml-2026-detecting-fluent-optimization-.tldr: A training-free detector tracks sequential entropy changes to identify fluent adversarial suffixes and localize where they begin.

paragraphs: Follow the regularized leader is widely used in online optimization, but its convergence speed in potential games has remained difficult to characterize. This paper establishes worst-case limits showing that the favorable structure of these games does not automatically make equilibrium learning fast. The results concern how long particular learning dynamics can take to reach a Nash equilibrium.

For two-player potential games, FTRL can require exponential convergence time with any permutation-invariant regularizer, including settings with potentially vanishing learning rates. Known equivalences transfer the lower bound to certain mirror descent methods, especially multiplicative weights update. The result therefore reaches beyond a single formulation of the learning rule.

The authors also establish a potential property for FTRL and an exponential upper bound for no-regret dynamics run in a lazy, alternating fashion, matching their lower bound up to factors in the exponent. For multiplayer potential games, fictitious play can take doubly exponential time. Together, the results distinguish the existence of convergence structure from the possibility of efficient convergence in the worst case.
icml-2026-doubly-exponential-lower-bound.tldr: FTRL can converge exponentially slowly in two-player potential games, while fictitious play can require doubly exponential time with multiple players.

paragraphs: Finding errors inside a long answer requires confidence measures that work at a finer scale than the entire response. Evaluating those measures becomes difficult when correctness labels themselves are unreliable. SALT addresses this problem with six procedurally generated tasks, each having one deterministic long textual answer, enabling evaluation without an external judge.

The benchmark supports measurements of correctness, calibration, and confidence ranking at different resolutions. Across more than 50 language models, the authors find that confidence ranking largely fails at the smallest atomic units, even when correct and incorrect content separates more clearly at the line level. A confidence measure that looks useful for larger passages may therefore be much less useful for locating individual errors.

Controlled interventions also distinguish error propagation from corrupted prefixes and bounded degradation as answer context grows longer. Global context correctness dominates the propagation effect. Finally, both prompted and trained reasoning improve accuracy while worsening confidence ranking in the analysis. These findings separate producing fewer mistakes from reliably identifying the mistakes that remain.
icml-2026-evaluating-llm-uncertainty-in-.tldr: SALT uses deterministic long answers to show that fine-grained error confidence can remain unreliable even as reasoning improves accuracy.

paragraphs: A machine-checked proof establishes a formal statement, but the statement may still misrepresent the intended mathematical problem. This paper audits that gap in Lean theorem-proving benchmarks. It also examines evaluation machinery, where trivial or adversarial solutions can undermine what a reported success actually measures.

The authors audit five widely used benchmarks and their forks using static checkers across the corpora. They surface 4,833 findings, including 398 mechanically certified issues involving counterexamples, vacuous theorems, and unsound axioms. Their semantic analysis also identifies missing assumptions, simplified problems, incorrect or incomplete translations, and hazards specific to Lean specifications.

Evaluations on corrected subsets show that dataset defects can push prover scores in either direction: they can make performance appear better or worse. The paper responds with a fault taxonomy, automated checkers, semantic-audit prompts designed to find more issues, and release standards. The contribution extends benchmark validation beyond proof acceptance to the meaning of the problem and the behavior of the evaluation process.
icml-2026-faults-in-our-formal-benchmark.tldr: An audit of Lean benchmarks shows that specification defects and evaluation failures can distort scores despite machine-checked proofs.

paragraphs: Diffusion models learn a score field whose behavior often approximately respects transformations such as flips, rotations, or circular shifts. GEPC uses that structure to detect unfamiliar inputs. It checks whether transforming an input changes the score in the corresponding expected way, looking for broken symmetry rather than relying only on score magnitude or local geometry.

The method averages transformation-consistency residuals over a finite group. It needs only score evaluations and requires no additional training. The authors also define an ideal population-level residual and derive upper bounds for in-distribution data and lower bounds for out-of-distribution data under their assumptions. These bounds provide theoretical support for using equivariance violations as a detection signal.

On image benchmarks, GEPC achieves competitive or improved AUROC against recent diffusion-based detectors while remaining computationally lightweight. On high-resolution synthetic aperture radar imagery, it separates targets or anomalies from background clutter. Its maps indicate where equivariance breaks, making the detection signal spatially interpretable as well as useful for distinguishing unfamiliar inputs.
icml-2026-gepc-group-equivariant-posteri.tldr: GEPC detects unfamiliar inputs by measuring whether a diffusion model's score field responds consistently to transformations.

paragraphs: Multimodal in-context learning supplies image-text demonstrations alongside a query, but those examples add inference latency and make results sensitive to their wording, order, and content. Hyper-ICL trains a model to reconstruct the demonstrations' effects so that examples are no longer required at inference time.

Its first component is a low-rank adapter that adjusts attention logits to reproduce the attention redistribution induced by demonstrations. A query-dependent mechanism controls how strongly those adjustments act on individual tokens across layers and attention heads. This lets the intervention vary with the current query instead of applying the same correction everywhere.

A second component distills intermediate features from a teacher that receives demonstrations. The layer-wise loss uses Lorentz geodesic distance in hyperbolic space to encourage preservation of demonstration–query relationships. Across six multimodal benchmarks, including visual question answering and image captioning, Hyper-ICL consistently improves accuracy and stability over vanilla in-context learning and the compared state-of-the-art methods. The approach transfers demonstration-conditioned behavior into trained adaptations that can operate without those demonstrations.
icml-2026-hyper-icl-attention-calibratio.tldr: Hyper-ICL learns query-adaptive attention corrections and teacher feature relationships to deliver multimodal demonstration effects without inference-time examples.

paragraphs: This paper strengthens machine-learning attacks on Learning with Errors settings that use binary or small secrets. Earlier attacks succeeded only on relatively simple secrets, including very few nonzero bits in the difficult region remaining after preprocessing. The authors investigate how training-data scale, repeated examples, and a separate recovery procedure extend that reach.

Larger training sets and repetition allow recovery of denser secrets. The authors empirically observe a power-law relationship involving model-based recovery attempts, dataset size, and repeated examples. They also introduce stepwise regression to recover the secret's so-called cool bits, combining improvements in the learned attack with an additional method for recovering part of the secret.

For binary secrets, the reported recoveries reach Hamming weight 70 with eight cruel bits at dimension 256, and weight 75 with seven cruel bits at dimension 512, at the specified moduli. Previous results cited in the abstract reached weights 33 and 63 with three cruel bits. The methods also improve recovery for denser ternary secrets, establishing stronger empirical attacks in the investigated settings.
icml-2026-improving-ml-attacks-on-lwe-wi.tldr: Larger datasets, repeated training examples, and stepwise regression enable ML attacks to recover denser LWE secrets in the tested settings.

paragraphs: Watermarking generated text can support both detection and attribution to a particular model or user. IPMark addresses the combined challenge of personalized attribution, efficient detection, text quality, and robustness. Its design links a structured identity system with a sentence-level method for inserting watermark signals.

The identity system uses a hierarchy inspired by IP addressing to organize model and user identities. This supports hierarchical retrieval during detection. For watermark insertion, IPMark selects among sentence candidates using two streams of features: semantic information about meaning and syntactic information about form. The authors use these complementary signals to reduce the semantic distortion associated with token-level watermarking.

In the reported experiments, IPMark has the lowest perplexity among the compared baselines, which the authors use as evidence of improved generation quality. It also maintains strong robustness and substantially reduces detection latency through hierarchical retrieval. The contribution is the joint design: sentence selection governs how the watermark enters text, while the identity hierarchy makes personalized attribution more efficient.
icml-2026-ipmark-a-sentence-level-waterm.tldr: IPMark combines sentence-level semantic and syntactic watermarking with hierarchical model and user identities for efficient personalized attribution.

paragraphs: Online covering algorithms must respond to requests as they arrive, without knowing the entire future sequence. This paper develops a general way to incorporate predictions about those requests into existing algorithms. The framework is black-box, allowing a prediction-aware method to be built from an online algorithm without redesigning its internal approach.

The main guarantee changes what drives the competitive ratio, a measure of performance against an offline optimum. If the original bound depends on the number of arriving requests, the transformed bound replaces that dependence with prediction error. Other arguments of the bound remain part of the guarantee, so the improvement specifically targets uncertainty about future requests.

With sufficiently accurate predictions, this can beat the corresponding worst-case lower bounds for online algorithms. As predictions worsen, the guarantee degrades smoothly with their error. The framework applies to facility location, Steiner problems, set cover, parking permits, and other covering problems, yielding improved and new bounds through one shared construction rather than separate prediction mechanisms for each problem.
icml-2026-learning-augmented-online-cove.tldr: A black-box framework converts online covering guarantees from dependence on request count to dependence on prediction error.

paragraphs: Quadratic discriminant analysis models each class with a Gaussian distribution, which can misrepresent data with heavy tails. This paper argues that correcting the likelihood model can matter more than replacing ordinary parameter estimates with robust ones. It introduces Stable-QDA to address that mismatch directly in the probabilities used for classification.

Stable-QDA replaces the Gaussian likelihood with a symmetric alpha-stable likelihood whose tails decay polynomially rather than exponentially with Mahalanobis distance. This changes how the classifier weighs observations far from a class center. The authors find that standard sample means and Ledoit–Wolf covariance estimates often outperform robust alternatives when differences in class variability help distinguish the classes.

The paper supplies consistency guarantees in infinite-variance regimes and data-driven diagnostics for choosing estimators. On real-world heavy-tailed benchmarks, it reports error reductions of 15–53%. The central finding is qualified but consequential: when class-dependent variability carries useful information, improving the distributional model can produce larger gains than robustifying estimation, and conventional estimators can remain effective within that improved model.
icml-2026-likelihood-over-estimation-rob.tldr: Stable-QDA improves heavy-tailed classification by changing the likelihood, finding that this can matter more than robust parameter estimation.

paragraphs: Malware classifiers trained on known samples can lose effectiveness as threats change. MalTree investigates evolutionary relationships among malware families to support analysis beyond classifying isolated samples. It automates lineage modeling, a task for which traditional reverse engineering can require months or years.

The framework applies two phylogenetic methods borrowed from bioinformatics, UPGMA and Neighbor-Joining, to structural, behavioral, and image-based features. These methods organize malware relationships into trees. The authors add temporal validation using VirusTotal timestamps, checking whether the inferred relationships agree with the order in which threats emerged.

MalTree achieves 87% temporal consistency, providing evidence that its inferred structure broadly aligns with emergence timelines. Its analysis finds that some families mutate more than ten times faster than others, suggesting value in adapting detection strategies to family-specific rates of change. Case studies including Mirai also agree with documented threat intelligence. Together, these results support lineage-aware analysis as a foundation for understanding malware evolution and informing more proactive defenses.
icml-2026-maltree-tracing-malware-evolut.tldr: MalTree builds malware lineage trees from multiple feature types and validates their alignment with emergence timelines and documented threat intelligence.

paragraphs: Decision-making under uncertainty often requires optimizing while the underlying distribution changes over time. Although non-parametric approaches had been developed for time-varying deterministic optimization, this paper extends that direction to stochastic problems. Its focus includes settings where the decisions themselves are stochastic, adding randomness to the objects being optimized.

The authors develop a stochastic variational framework using Malliavin calculus. It provides non-parametric optimality conditions and supports a deep-learning algorithm called Stochastic Path Follower. The framework is designed to make the algorithm insensitive to the dimension of the parameterization, addressing scalability alongside the problem of adapting to changing distributions.

The experiments apply Stochastic Path Follower to least-squares recovery and logistic regression under distribution drift. In these evaluations, it outperforms the compared state-of-the-art learning-based and gradient-based approaches in performance and scalability. The contribution connects a mathematical extension of non-parametric optimization to a practical learning method, showing how optimality conditions for stochastic decisions can guide computation in changing environments.
icml-2026-non-parametric-optimization-fo.tldr: A stochastic variational framework yields Stochastic Path Follower, a scalable learning algorithm evaluated on optimization problems under distribution drift.

paragraphs: In performative prediction, deploying a model changes the data distribution on which it will subsequently operate. Simple retraining is known to converge linearly when these feedback effects are weak. This paper studies the computational difficulty once the feedback-strength parameter crosses above one, where the general complexity had remained unresolved.

The authors prove that finding an approximately performatively stable point is PPAD-complete, placing it in the same polynomial-time complexity class as computing Nash equilibria in general-sum games. The hardness appears even when feedback exceeds the threshold by only an amount proportional to the approximation tolerance. It also persists with quadratic losses and linear distribution shifts.

A technical extension establishes PPAD-hardness on general convex domains, contributing to the broader study of variational inequalities. For strategic classification, the authors additionally show that finding a strategic local optimum is PLS-hard. These are worst-case computational barriers: even simple-looking ingredients can produce difficult feedback problems, sharply separating the weak-feedback convergence regime from the regime just beyond its threshold.
icml-2026-on-the-computational-complexit.tldr: Computing approximate performative stability becomes PPAD-complete just beyond the weak-feedback regime, even with quadratic losses and linear shifts.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes a mathematical view of Transformer computation in which token embeddings behave like interacting particles. Layers play the role of time, and embeddings move on a unit sphere that idealizes layer normalization. This perspective turns the forward pass into a dynamical system whose collective behavior can be studied geometrically.

For some weight settings, that system follows the gradient of an explicit energy function. Wasserstein gradient flows then provide a way to describe a mean-field limit as context length becomes infinite. Within this setting, the authors focus on the effect of the perceptron block on the resulting landscape.

Their main result is that critical points are generically atomic and localized on subsets of the sphere. In this description, the limiting token distribution concentrates into point masses rather than spreading continuously across the sphere. The finding characterizes the structure of critical configurations in the studied model. It connects the perceptron block to where token mass can concentrate within this idealized account of attention dynamics.
icml-2026-perceptrons-and-localization-o.tldr: In an idealized mean-field Transformer model, the perceptron block yields critical points that are generically atomic and spatially localized.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning aims to remove the influence of selected training data while preserving useful behavior. This paper moves the intervention into the model's representation space. It learns a transformation of representations, addressing instability, computational expense, and local-approximation constraints associated with approaches that update the underlying model's parameters.

The transformation implements an information bottleneck: its objective encourages information about retained data while suppressing information about the data designated for forgetting. Because that information-based objective is difficult to optimize directly, the authors derive tractable variational surrogates. These provide practical ways to train the transformation while preserving the intended balance between retention and forgetting.

The framework covers two data-access regimes: one with both retain and forget data, and a zero-shot regime with access only to forget data. Across several benchmarks, the authors report more reliable forgetting, better preservation of utility, and greater computational efficiency than parameter-centric baselines. The findings support representation transformation as an alternative place to carry out selective forgetting while maintaining useful model behavior.
icml-2026-representation-unlearning-forg.tldr: Representation Unlearning learns an information-compressing transformation that suppresses forget-data information while preserving useful retained information.

paragraphs: People can respond strategically to an algorithm by changing their inputs to obtain more favorable decisions. Those changes carry costs, and strategic classification tries to account for them when designing the classifier. This paper examines a feedback effect: the algorithm's current decisions can change how costly manipulation becomes in the future.

Existing approaches described in the abstract assume that manipulation costs are fixed and independent of classifier decisions. The authors replace that assumption with a two-stage robust optimization framework. Its uncertainty set depends on the decision, allowing the range of possible future costs to change with the policy chosen today.

This formulation makes the consequences of a policy part of the uncertainty the algorithm must manage. The paper's analysis highlights that recognizing policy-dependent costs can both reduce uncertainty and better restrain gaming over time. The contribution is a model of strategic behavior in which the classifier influences future incentives, rather than treating manipulation costs as an external quantity that stays unchanged as decisions accumulate.
icml-2026-robust-strategic-classificatio.tldr: A two-stage robust framework models how classifier decisions change future manipulation costs and can help curb strategic gaming over time.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can recognize individual concepts yet mishandle a request such as finding an umbrella with no person present. This paper traces that failure to the similarity interface: scores tend to pool evidence for concepts without adequately enforcing the operators connecting them. Signals about those operators exist in text embeddings but are too weak or misaligned to reliably change rankings.

The proposed factored inference approach separates obtaining concept evidence from executing constraints. Its LCSE method uses concept scores from frozen encoders and applies the constraints externally, requiring no training. This targets the aggregation bottleneck that the authors find fine-tuning does not reliably resolve.

On the introduced FACTOR-Bench, LCSE achieves 85.5% accuracy against 73.2% for the best fine-tuned baseline, and reaches 90.7% with SigLIP 2. It also raises NegBench COCO multiple-choice accuracy from 27.2% to 65.2% while preserving retrieval performance. The results show that changing how existing concept evidence is used can substantially improve compliance with compositional queries.
icml-2026-similarity-is-not-logic-factor.tldr: LCSE improves compositional image retrieval by extracting concept scores from frozen encoders and enforcing logical constraints separately.

paragraphs: A digital twin can help choose policies by simulating their consequences, yet accurate prediction of individual transitions may not produce accurate policy rankings. This paper proves that mismatch can arise when model capacity is limited and observes it empirically even with expressive model classes. The training objective can therefore be poorly aligned with the decision the simulation is intended to support.

DT² trains digital twins directly to preserve policy rankings. It first uses fitted Q-evaluation on offline data to estimate candidate policy values. Those estimates serve as proxy ground truth, and an architecture-agnostic loss trains simulated rollouts to preserve the corresponding pairwise ordering of policies.

Across the evaluated settings and architectures, DT² improves policy ranking and reduces decision regret relative to conventional digital-twin training. The improvements hold for policies included during training and for unseen policies, while retaining good raw simulation fidelity. The approach makes the downstream choice explicit in training, using estimated policy comparisons to shape a simulator that is useful for selecting among alternatives.
icml-2026-textdt-text2-decision-targeted.tldr: DT² trains digital twins to preserve estimated policy rankings, improving policy selection while maintaining good simulation fidelity.

paragraphs: Tokenizers determine the units through which language models represent and process text. Their effect is difficult to isolate when models also differ in architecture, training data, or training budget. TokSuite provides a controlled collection of models and a benchmark designed to make tokenizer choice a more directly measurable source of behavioral differences.

The collection contains fourteen pretrained models using different off-the-shelf tokenizers. Architecture, dataset, training budget, and initialization are held constant across the models. This shared setup supports comparisons in which differences are attributable more directly to tokenization than comparisons among independently developed language models would allow.

TokSuite also includes a multilingual robustness benchmark covering English, Chinese, Farsi, Italian, and Turkish. Native annotators curate real-world text perturbations to assess how model performance responds to changes in input. Together, the controlled models and benchmark support findings about the benefits and shortcomings of popular tokenizers. The contribution is an experimental resource for studying tokenization's influence on both performance and robustness across multiple languages.
icml-2026-toksuite-measuring-the-impact-.tldr: TokSuite isolates tokenizer effects with fourteen otherwise matched language models and a five-language robustness benchmark.

paragraphs: Learning-rate warm-up starts training with small updates and increases their size over an initial period. This paper explains that practice through the curvature of the optimization landscape. It develops a smoothness condition that bounds local curvature using a linear function of how far the loss is from its optimal value.

The condition generalizes an existing smoothness framework and has closure properties that support its use in analysis. The authors provide theoretical and empirical evidence that common neural architectures satisfy it and that it describes curvature early in training. Adapting the learning rate to this condition naturally produces a schedule resembling warm-up.

Under the proposed analysis, the resulting schedule has provably faster convergence guarantees than a fixed learning rate. Experiments on language and vision models show that its one-parameter form can match tuned linear warm-up and improve over training without warm-up. The contribution connects a widely used training practice to an explicit curvature model, while also producing a simple schedule that performs competitively in the reported evaluations.
icml-2026-why-do-we-need-warm-up-a-theor.tldr: A curvature-based smoothness analysis yields a warm-up-like learning-rate schedule with faster convergence guarantees and competitive empirical performance.
